data_evidence: registered users represented 81.17% of recorded rentals.
operational_implication: Demand planning can distinguish between casual and registered user needs rather than treating all rentals as one market.
interpretation_limit: Rental records do not identify unique users or individual customer motives.

data_evidence: Average daily rentals changed by 64.43% from 2011 to 2012.
operational_implication: Capacity and service planning should account for the change in demand level between years.
interpretation_limit: The dataset does not explain what caused the annual change.

data_evidence: Peak months — 2011: june (4783.73); 2012: september (7285.77). Peak seasons — 2011: fall (4464.36); 2012: fall (6824.24).
operational_implication: Higher-demand periods can inform capacity planning, while lower-demand periods may be more suitable for planned maintenance.
interpretation_limit: Month and season overlap with weather, holidays, and annual growth.

data_evidence: Peak hours were 17:00 for total demand, 14:00 for casual users, and 17:00 for registered users.
operational_implication: Bike availability, station readiness, and rebalancing can be scheduled before the identified peak periods.
interpretation_limit: Trip purpose is not recorded, so commuting and leisure interpretations remain inferred.

data_evidence: Casual users represented 13.23% of working-day rentals and 31.66% of non-working-day rentals.
operational_implication: Working and non-working days should use different operating profiles because user composition is not identical.
interpretation_limit: Non-working days combine weekends and official holidays.

data_evidence: The strongest selected Spearman association was between temp_c and casual (0.667).
operational_implication: Weather information can support short-term planning, but it should be combined with calendar and seasonal information.
interpretation_limit: Association does not establish causation, and weather variables may overlap.
